title: Synthesis of oocyte-specific proteins during mouse embryogenesis and biological significance thereof
projectDescription: The genes of the zona pellucida (Zp) encode for the glycoproteins that form the extracellular coat surrounding and protecting the mammalian oocyte. These genes are four in humans (Zp1-4), three in mice (Zp1-3) due to pseudogene conversion of one of the four genes. Zp genes are regarded as quintessential members of the family of oocyte-specific genes, that is: transcription is silenced by the end of oogenesis, and this inactive state is preserved also after fertilization, in the embryos. The proteins that were synthesized during oogenesis are passed on to the embryos, and the residual Zp mRNAs that were made before gene silencing are thought to fade away without serving any embryonic role. It follows that the amount of ZP proteins in embryos should not increase, but rather decrease. Contrary to this widespread notion, we observed in mice that the abundance of all three ZP proteins increased during preimplantation development, peaking at the 8-cell stage, as measured by two orthogonal methods (immunofluorescence with directly labeled primary antibody, and mass spectrometry). We thus hypothesized that there may be de novo synthesis of ZP proteins during preimplantation development, and that ZP proteins may serve hitherto unknown developmental functions. If that were the case, it would mean that genes considered oocyte-specific are not such anymore – at least not from a protein standpoint. We reasoned that if there is a new synthesis of ZP proteins during embryogenesis, there is probably also a function associated with it. We tested this possibility by depleting the protein, directing the Trim-Away method of protein degradation to the ZP2 of wild-type zygotes (B6C3F1 x CD1). Trim-Away works by microinjecting the cell with an antibody directed against a protein of interest and with the mRNA encoding the ubiquitin-protein ligase Trim21. After microinjection of zygotes with anti-ZP2 antibody (ATCC IE-3) and Trim21 mRNA we observed no impressive phenotype, except that the embryos were delayed at morula-to-blastocyst transition, although in the end they formed blastocysts nonetheless. We posited that perhaps the amount of ZP2 we removed with Trim-away was replenished by de novo synthesis of ZP2 protein, consistent with the observation of the peak of ZP2 protein at the 8-cell stage. To test this alluring possibility, in addition to depleting ZP2 with Trim-Away we also inhibited ZP2 protein synthesis. To this end, we combined Trim-away with an antisense morpholino oligonucleotide (MO) that inhibits Zp2 mRNA translation (MO sequence derived from PMID 7822321). The phenotype became more severe, with defects of cell lineage composition in the blastocysts depleted of ZP2. We generated three experimental groups, in parallel, as follows: 1) KNOCKDOWN of ZP2, by zygote microinjection of Trim21 mRNA in conjunction with anti-ZP2 antibody (Trim-away) plus MO anti-ZP2; 2) MOCK KNOCKDOWN, in which both the antibody and the MO were directed against an irrelevant protein, namely GFP; 3) MICROMANIPULATION CONTROL, by zygote microinjection of sole Trim21 mRNA. In these three groups we expected to measure the native amount of ZP2 (group 3), a possible non-specific effect of Trim-away and morpholino on ZP2 (group 2), and a reduced amount of ZP2 due to Trim-Away of ZP2 reinforced by inhibition of de novo ZP2 synthesis (group 1). The microinjected zygotes were cultured in KSOM medium containing amino acids. Morulae were collected from each group on day 3, deprived of the outer zona pellucida by washing in Tyrode solution, and lysed in iST PreOmics buffer. We conducted a total of 4 experiments in each of which, each time, all three groups were represented with approximately the same numbers of embryos per group (approximately 40). The 12 samples were processed by mass spectrometry as per our established pipeline. This dataset offers us a measure of the efficiency of Trim-Away and morpholino combined as applied to ZP2, and reveals a previously unanticipated role of embryonic ZP2 during early stages of mouse development.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Morulae were collected from each group on day 3, deprived of the outer zona pellucida by washing in Tyrode solution, lysed in PreOmics iST LYSE buffer and stored at -20°C until further processing. Lysates were processed using the PreOmics iST kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Purified peptides were dissolved in 10 µl LC-LOAD loading buffer, and 1 µl was used for subsequent mass spectrometry analysis. Nanoflow reversed-phase liquid chromatography was performed using a nanoElute 2 UHPLC system (Bruker Daltonics), coupled online to a timsTOF Pro2 mass spectrometer via a CaptiveSpray nano-electrospray ion source (Bruker Daltonics). Peptide separation was achieved using a 25 cm × 75 µm fused silica capillary column (CoAnn Technologies), home-packed with 1.5 µm ReproSil Saphir 100 C18 beads (Dr. Maisch). To elute bound peptides a linear gradient of 4–27% buffer B (99.9% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid) over 60 minutes was applied, with buffer A consisting of 0.1% formic acid. The flow rate was set to 300 nl/min. The mass spectrometer was operated in DIA-PASEF mode using the standard DIA-PASEF long-gradient method. Signals were recorded across a mass range of 100–1700 m/z and an ion mobility range from 1/K₀ = 0.60 to 1.65 Vs/cm², with a ramp time of 100 ms in the dual TIMS analyzer. Collision energy was adjusted as a function of ion mobility, ranging from 59 eV at 1/K₀ = 1.60 Vs/cm² to 20 eV at 1/K₀ = 0.6 Vs/cm².
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw mass spectrometry data were processed using DIA-NN software (v2.0.2) in library-free search mode with heuristic protein inference performed at the gene level. Neural networks were employed in single-pass mode, enabling matching between runs, and QuantUMS was applied as the quantification strategy. The predicted library included entries sourced from mouse UniProt UP000000589_10090_additional.fasta database (April 2024 version), including isoforms, the mCherry sequence, and common laboratory contaminants. Search parameters included carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues as a fixed modification, while oxidation of methionine and acetylation of protein N-termini were set as variable modifications. Trypsin was specified as the digesting enzyme, allowing up to two missed cleavages and peptides with lengths between 7–30 amino acids. Mass tolerances were set to 20 ppm for MS scans and 15 ppm for MS/MS scans, with charges above +4 excluded from analysis. Protein groups were considered identified with a false discovery rate (FDR) of ≤1% at both peptide and protein levels. Initial downstream analysis was performed using Perseus software (v1.6.15.0). Common laboratory contaminants were removed from the dataset, and protein intensity values provided in the pg_matrix.tsv table were log₂-transformed. Summary statistics for samples and protein groups were generated to provide a first overview of the dataset.
